records.sourceFile: Effect of Individual Environmental Heat-Stress Variables on Training and Recovery in Professional Team Sport.pdf

paper.citation: O'Connor FK, Stern SE, Doering TM, Minett GM, Reaburn PR, Bartlett JD, et al. Effect of Individual Environmental Heat-Stress Variables on Training and Recovery in Professional Team Sport. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Forty-five professional Australian Rules football players were monitored across 579 outdoor training sessions in an 8-week preseason. Solar radiation, relative humidity and ambient temperature were each related to GPS external load, heart rate, RPE, well-being and heart-rate variability using mixed-effects models.
paper.tldr: In heat-acclimatized professional footballers, higher solar radiation was associated with less distance and high-speed running in training, and higher humidity with higher RPE and stress. Higher ambient temperature was associated with more work. Recovery links were weak.
paper.methods: Prospective observational study of 45 male professional Australian Rules football players during an 8-week preseason. Ambient temperature, humidity and solar radiation were measured at each outdoor session. GPS (distance per minute, percentage of distance above 14.4 km/h), heart-rate zones, RPE, well-being and daily rMSSD were analyzed with mixed-effects linear models, with the player as a random effect and standardized coefficients reported.
paper.findings: Solar radiation was associated with lower distance per minute (-19.7 m/min, P < .001) and lower percentage high-speed running (-10.1%, P < .001), and with lower rMSSD 48 hours after training (-16.9 ms, P = .019). Relative humidity was associated with lower high-speed running (-3.4%, P = .010), more time above 85% HRmax (+3.9%, P < .001), higher RPE (+1.8 AU, P < .001), greater body mass loss (-215 g, P < .001) and more stress 24 hours after training (-0.11 AU on the well-being scale, P = .002). Higher ambient temperature was associated with more distance (+19.2 m/min, P < .001) and high-speed running (+3.5%, P = .005), alongside higher mean heart rate (+4.8 bpm, P < .001) and slightly higher RPE (+0.3 AU, P = .019).
paper.limitations: The design is observational, using a convenience sample of heat-acclimatized players from one club in one subtropical preseason, and the authors state they cannot ascribe cause and effect. The abstract gives the temperature effect on distance as 19.7 m/min while the results text gives 19.2 m/min (95% CI 18.0 to 21.4); the results value is reported here. Recovery links were mostly null, and heart-rate variability was measured once each morning with a smartphone application.
paper.practicalImplications: In hot preseason training, staff should record solar radiation and humidity separately, because the study links each to different training outcomes. Use the associations to plan and interpret sessions in the heat, not as fixed thresholds or proven causes of lost work capacity.
paper.athleteDev: The study measures training output in hot outdoor conditions, so it may guide how staff interpret GPS and heart-rate data across different weather. It does not test a training method or show that heat exposure improves performance, though the authors suggest higher temperature may relate to more work.
paper.rtp: The study does not address injury rehabilitation or return to play. It describes training load and recovery in heat-acclimatized squads, so it does not set criteria for clearing players after injury.

records.sourceFile: Effect of velocity loss during squat training on neuromuscular performance.pdf

paper.citation: Rodríguez-Rosell D, Yáñez-García JM, Mora-Custodio R, Sánchez-Medina L, Ribas-Serna J, González-Badillo JJ. Effect of velocity loss during squat training on neuromuscular performance. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2021;00:1-15.
paper.abstract: Thirty-three young men were randomly assigned to 8 weeks of velocity-based squat training with velocity losses of 10%, 30% or 45% allowed in each set, with identical loads, frequency and rest. All groups improved strength and muscle endurance. The 10% group showed the greatest countermovement jump and sprint improvements, and the authors conclude that a low velocity-loss limit gives similar strength gains with better jump and sprint gains than higher limits.
paper.tldr: In 33 physically active young men training squats twice weekly for 8 weeks, limiting each set to 10% velocity loss gave strength gains similar to 30% and 45% limits with about a third to half the repetitions, and a larger jump gain than the 45% limit. Sprint differences between groups were not statistically confirmed, and the study used one exercise, so it does not show that 10% is optimal for all athletes.
paper.methods: Randomized trial of three 8-week velocity-based squat programs, run twice weekly with 3 sets at 55 to 70% 1RM and 4 minutes of rest, differing only in the velocity loss allowed per set (10%, 30% or 45%). Sets ended when the target loss was reached, using a linear velocity transducer for feedback. Before and after training, participants completed a 20 m sprint, countermovement jump, progressive squat loading (estimated 1RM and load-velocity profile), a squat fatigue test and surface EMG of the vastus lateralis and medialis.
paper.findings: All groups improved estimated 1RM, load-velocity measures and fatigue test performance. The only significant group by time interaction was for countermovement jump, where the 10% group's gain (11.9%, effect size 0.75) was significantly larger than the 45% group's; for 20 m sprint the 10% group improved significantly within group (-2.4% to -3.1% across 10 and 20 m), the 30% group improved at 20 m but not 10 m, and the 45% group did not improve, but no significant interaction was reported. The 10% group completed about 181 repetitions over the program compared with about 348 in the 30% group and 501 in the 45% group, and no EMG variable changed significantly in any group.
paper.limitations: The study had no non-training control group, included only young men who were physically active students, and used one exercise (Smith machine squat), so its scope is limited to these conditions. The Abstract says the 10% group's jump gain was greater than both other groups and that its sprint change was greater, but the Results report a significant between-group difference in jump height only against the 45% group and a significant interaction only for jump. Strength was estimated from a load-velocity equation rather than measured as a direct 1RM, and the surface EMG findings cannot rule out changes in muscles not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: For squat programs in young, moderately trained men, stopping each set at a 10% velocity loss gave similar strength gains to 30% or 45% limits with far fewer repetitions, and a larger jump gain than the 45% limit, in this 8-week study. Velocity monitoring can be used to stop sets at a chosen loss, but the study does not show that 10% is optimal for every athlete or sport, or that it improves sprinting more than higher limits.
paper.athleteDev: Coaches can use a velocity-loss cap, set at 10% in this study, to limit fatigue and repetitions within squat sets while keeping strength gains and supporting jump improvement. The trial measured squat strength, jump and sprint outcomes in non-athletes, not sport-specific performance, and sprint differences between groups were not statistically confirmed.
paper.rtp: The trial used healthy, injury-free young men and did not test rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot support using velocity-loss limits to guide injury rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Effectiveness of Accentuated Eccentric Loading - Contingent on Concentric Load.pdf

paper.citation: Merrigan JJ, Tufano JJ, Falzone M, Jones MT. Effectiveness of Accentuated Eccentric Loading: Contingent on Concentric Load. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Crossover study of 21 resistance-trained men comparing a single accentuated eccentric repetition (120% 1-RM) with traditional loading during back-squat sets at 65% and 80% 1-RM. Eccentric velocity and power were greater after AEL, and the concentric benefit appeared only at the 65% load, where velocity and power were higher in later repetitions.
paper.tldr: In resistance-trained men, one 120% 1-RM eccentric repetition improved later back-squat velocity and power at a 65% 1-RM working load but not at 80% 1-RM. Eccentric power was higher after AEL at both loads, so the concentric benefit depends on the working load.
paper.methods: Four sessions, 48 h apart, in a counterbalanced crossover: AEL65 (3 x 5 at 120%/65% 1-RM), AEL80 (3 x 3 at 120%/80%), TRA65 and TRA80 at matched loads. Weight releasers disengaged after the first eccentric phase; a force plate and four linear position transducers measured kinetics and kinematics, analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: At 65%, AEL produced higher eccentric peak velocity (-0.076 m/s, P = .01) and greater eccentric power than TRA65 (eccentric peak power -328.6 W, P < .01), and concentric peak force was 187.8 N higher (95% CI 58.5 to 317.1). Concentric velocity and mean power were higher only in repetitions 3 and 4. At 80%, concentric peak force was 133.8 N higher with AEL and eccentric mean and peak power were greater, but concentric velocity and power did not increase, and concentric mean velocity in repetition 1 was lower.
paper.limitations: Only 21 men, one session per protocol, and lab measures only. The abstract gives P = .01 for the 65% concentric peak force difference, while the Results give P < .01; the Results value is reported here. The Results also show a significant protocol-by-repetition effect for concentric mean power at 80%, but the Discussion states no concentric power increase occurred at 80%; the Discussion statement is reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: A single 120% eccentric overload before 65% 1-RM squat sets was followed by higher velocity and power in later repetitions in this sample, so it may be worth testing in that context. The study found no concentric velocity or power gain at 80% 1-RM, so the same protocol should not be expected to improve heavy sets. At 80% 1-RM the concentric mean velocity of the first repetition was lower after AEL, which the authors attribute to an altered pacing strategy when controlling the weight releasers.
paper.athleteDev: In these resistance-trained men, a single 120% 1-RM eccentric overload improved later back-squat velocity and power at 65% 1-RM but not at 80% 1-RM. Staff should treat the load-dependence as the main finding, since the effects came from one acute session.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy resistance-trained men in one acute session and included no injured or rehabilitating athletes.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Resistance and Speed on Electromyographic Activity of Thigh and Gluteal Muscles in Elite Athletes throughout Resisted Sprint Running.pdf

paper.citation: Macchi R, Hegyi A, Giroux C, Rabita G, Nordez A, Hollville E, et al. Effects of Resistance and Speed on Electromyographic Activity of Thigh and Gluteal Muscles in Elite Athletes throughout Resisted Sprint Running. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025 (published ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Within-session study of 37 elite athletes measuring surface EMG from eight thigh and gluteal muscles during unresisted sprints and sprints against resistance equal to 25% and 75% of body mass. Hamstring activity rose with speed and fell with resistance, the reverse of the quadriceps pattern, and the response differed between hamstring heads.
paper.tldr: In elite track and field, rugby sevens and bobsleigh athletes, hamstring muscle activity rose with running speed and fell with added resistance, while quadriceps showed the opposite pattern. The response differed between hamstring muscles, but the study measured activation in one session and does not show any training benefit.
paper.methods: Each athlete completed two trials of a 40 m unresisted sprint and sprints with robotic resistance equal to 25% and 75% of body mass (sled-equivalent; 25 m and 20 m sprints), with force plates, optoelectronic timing and EMG on eight muscles per leg. Generalized mixed models related EMG to normalised speed in stance and swing phases, statistical parametric mapping tested sprint phase and resistance across the stride, and binomial tests assessed between-athlete consistency.
paper.findings: Hamstring stance-phase EMG rose with speed in the unresisted sprint (+17.9%, P < 0.001) and was lower at higher resistance for all hamstring muscles except short head biceps femoris, while quadriceps showed higher stance activity at higher resistance. Between-athlete consistency for hamstring stance-phase increases with speed was high in unresisted and low-resistance sprints (89% to 100% in Table 2), but fell to 60% to 66% for semimembranosus and semitendinosus at the highest resistance, which was not significantly different from 50%. In the unresisted sprint, biceps femoris long head was the only hamstring head with higher late-swing activity at maximum speed and late acceleration than in early acceleration.
paper.limitations: Surface EMG may include cross-talk and cannot show neural drive directly, and the study used two resistance levels and compared conditions at normalised speed rather than absolute speed. The Discussion states consistent hamstring increases in 90% of athletes, but the Results give a range of 70% to 100% and Table 2 shows 60% to 66% for semimembranosus and semitendinosus at the highest resistance; the Table values are reported here. The authors' suggestion that resisted sprinting could be introduced earlier after hamstring injury was not tested in injured athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Resisted sprints produced a different muscle activation pattern from unresisted sprints, with relatively more quadriceps and less hamstring activation, so they could be considered for targeting early acceleration. Whether this improves acceleration or lowers hamstring load was not tested. The study's gluteus medius finding is EMG only and does not show that gluteus medius exercises improve sprinting.
paper.athleteDev: Resistance and speed shifted hamstring and quadriceps activity in opposite directions, so the resistance level changes which thigh muscles are most active during a sprint. Whether matching resistance to a given acceleration phase improves performance was not tested; these are single-session EMG patterns.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested injury-free athletes in one session, and the suggestion that resisted sprinting could be introduced earlier after hamstring injury was not tested.

records.sourceFile: Effects of forearm wearable resistance during accelerated sprints - From a standing start position.pdf

paper.citation: Uthoff AM, Macadam P, Zois J, Nagahara R, Neville J, Cronin JB. Effects of forearm wearable resistance during accelerated sprints: From a standing start position. J Sports Sci. 2021.
paper.abstract: Fourteen sprint-trained men completed 30 m sprints from a standing two-point start with and without 2 percent body mass of forearm wearable resistance. Sprint time at 10 m and 30 m did not change significantly, but step frequency fell in acceleration phases 2 and 3. The authors conclude that arm loading may provide a sprint-specific overload for two-point starts.
paper.tldr: Adding 2 percent body mass to the forearms did not significantly change 10 m or 30 m sprint time in trained male sprinters, but it lowered step frequency in the early-middle acceleration phases. Whether this helps performance over time was not tested.
paper.methods: Fourteen male track and field athletes completed three 30 m sprints from a standing two-point start over in-ground force plates: one unloaded and two with 2 percent body mass split between both forearms, with the loaded pair done before or after the unloaded trial in randomized order and the faster loaded trial analysed. Step kinematics and kinetics were averaged over four-step blocks from steps 1 to 16 and compared with a 2 x 4 repeated-measures ANOVA, with Cohen's d effect sizes.
paper.findings: Sprint times were not significantly different at 10 m (2.22 versus 2.26 s, effect size -0.32) or 30 m (4.60 versus 4.64 s, effect size -0.24). Step frequency decreased significantly in phase 2 (4.39 to 4.24 Hz, effect size -0.81) and phase 3 (4.44 to 4.28 Hz, effect size -0.86). Contact time, flight time, step length and vertical impulse rose with small to moderate effect sizes, but these were not reported as significant and no kinetic difference was statistically significant.
paper.limitations: This is a single-session, 14-man acute comparison with one unloaded trial and no training outcome, although the authors call it cross-sectional. The abstract reports a significant 3.6 percent step velocity drop in phase 4, but Table 2 shows no significant change (8.85 to 8.80 m/s, effect size -0.16); Table 1 percent-change intervals and several Table 2 contact time intervals exclude zero although the text calls them non-significant, while the starred step frequency effect size intervals include zero. One author is head of research at the garment manufacturer, though the authors state he was blinded from data collection and analysis.
paper.practicalImplications: Forearm loads of about 2 percent body mass did not significantly slow 10 m or 30 m sprint time in these sprint-trained men in one session. The lower step frequency in early and mid acceleration suggests the loads change step mechanics, but this should be treated as a hypothesis to test in a training block before it is used to target specific mechanics.
paper.athleteDev: Forearm wearable resistance at 2 percent body mass changed step frequency and contact and flight times in the first 16 steps without a clear loss of sprint time. Whether repeated training with these loads improves acceleration or sprint performance was not tested.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy, uninjured male athletes in a single session and does not address rehabilitation or return to sprinting after injury. It cannot be used to guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Effects of horizontally vs vertically loaded resistance exercises on performance and muscle architecture.pdf

paper.citation: Bartolomei S, Rosaci G, Latini D, Nigro F. Effects of horizontally versus vertically loaded resistance exercises on performance and muscle architecture. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2024.
paper.abstract: Nineteen resistance-trained adults were randomly assigned to six weeks of horizontally loaded (n = 10) or vertically loaded (n = 9) lower-body training with equal total repetitions. Horizontal training produced larger gains in 1RM hip thrust and standing long jump, while vertical training produced larger gains in 1RM squat and vastus medialis thickness. Countermovement jump showed only a small time effect with no group difference, and 20 m sprint did not change in either group.
paper.tldr: In resistance-trained adults, six weeks of hip-thrust-based training improved hip thrust strength and standing long jump more than squat-based training did, while squat-based training improved squat strength more. Neither program changed sprint time, and the study is too small, short and inconsistently reported to set training priorities.
paper.methods: Nineteen resistance-trained adults were randomly assigned to horizontally loaded (hip thrust, reverse hyperextension, horizontal jumps) or vertically loaded (parallel squat, barbell step-up, countermovement jumps) lower-body programs, four sessions per week for six weeks, with the same upper-body exercises and equal total repetitions. Pre and post measures included 1RM squat and hip thrust, countermovement jump, standing long jump, 20 m sprint, and ultrasound muscle thickness and echo intensity of the vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and gluteus.
paper.findings: Group by time interactions were significant for 1RM squat (P = 0.007), 1RM hip thrust (P = 0.004), standing long jump (P = 0.026) and vastus medialis thickness (P = 0.009). From Table III means, 1RM hip thrust rose 21.0 percent (horizontal) versus 1.8 percent (vertical) and 1RM squat rose 9.0 percent (vertical) versus -0.3 percent (horizontal); the text reports 17.9 versus 5.3 percent and 10.5 versus 0.1 percent. Countermovement jump had only a time main effect (P = 0.047; mean changes about 0.6 to 1.3 cm, below the stated 5.4 cm minimal difference), 20 m sprint did not change, and gluteus thickness rose over time without a group difference.
paper.limitations: The groups were small (9 and 10 analyzed versus 11 per group planned) and the program lasted only six weeks. Text percentages differ from Table III and IV means, the Discussion gives gluteus thickness gains of 14.8 and 18.0 percent while Table IV implies about 14 and 3 percent, the abstract gives p = 0.004 for the standing long jump interaction while Results give P = 0.026, the 1RM squat interaction effect size is 0.998, and some p-values (gluteus echo intensity F = 10.9 with P = 0.050; r = -0.487 with P = 0.004 in 19 people) do not match their statistics. Group characteristics also differ between the abstract and Methods.
paper.practicalImplications: If the goal is hip thrust strength or standing long jump, horizontally loaded exercises may be a useful choice, and squat-based work may suit squat strength and vastus medialis thickness. Neither program improved sprint time, and vertical jump changes were small in both. Given the small sample and reporting errors, these results should be tested in the target athletes before a program is chosen on their basis.
paper.athleteDev: Horizontal lower-body exercises such as hip thrust and reverse hyperextension favored standing long jump and hip thrust strength, while squat and step-up work favored squat strength in this six-week trial in resistance-trained adults. Neither program changed 20 m sprint time, so this study gives no basis for using either to improve sprinting.
paper.rtp: The participants were resistance-trained adults without an injury focus, and the study did not test injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes. It cannot be used to guide loading after a hamstring, hip or knee injury or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Effects of resistance exercise combined with vascular     occlusion on muscle function in athletes..pdf

paper.citation: Takarada Y, Sato Y, Ishii N. Effects of resistance exercise combined with vascular occlusion on muscle function in athletes. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2002;86:308-314.
paper.abstract: Elite rugby players completed 8 weeks of knee extension training at about 50% of 1RM with vascular occlusion (LIO, n = 6), the same load without occlusion (LI, n = 6), or no training (control, n = 5). The LIO group showed larger increases in isokinetic knee extension torque than the other two groups, a 12.3% increase in knee extensor cross-sectional area, and improved fatigue resistance, while the LI group showed no significant strength change.
paper.tldr: In 17 elite rugby players, eight weeks of knee extension at about 50% of 1RM with vascular occlusion increased quadriceps size, strength and fatigue resistance. The same load without occlusion did not increase strength, but the groups were small and not described as randomized.
paper.methods: Seventeen young male rugby players were assigned to LIO (about 50% 1RM with pneumatic thigh compression, mean 196 mmHg), LI (same load and repetitions without compression), or an untrained control group, all with more than 5 years of resistance-training history. Training ran twice weekly for 8 weeks, with four sets per session. Outcomes were isokinetic and isometric knee extension torque, knee extensor cross-sectional area by MRI (LIO only), fatigue indices over 50 contractions at 180 deg/s, and integrated EMG.
paper.findings: Averaged across velocities, strength rose 14.3 +/- 2.0% in LIO and 3.2 +/- 2.3% in LI, with LIO significantly greater at all velocities. Knee extensor cross-sectional area rose 12.3 +/- 0.8% in LIO (p = 0.002), while flexor and femur areas did not change. Fatigue indices fell from 63.7% to 58.7% and from 61.3% to 53.7% after LIO (p = 0.002 for both), with no change in LI or controls. Integrated EMG did not change in either the LIO or control group, and maximal isometric torque per unit area did not change.
paper.limitations: Five or six players per group, with no randomization described, and MRI measured only in the occlusion group. The control group was drawn from the same athlete pool and did not train, so the term 'untrained' refers to no study training. The results rest on one 8-week block of isokinetic and MRI measures, with no sport-specific performance, tendon or injury outcome. The Discussion's mechanisms (metabolic, hormonal, fibre-type) were not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: In highly trained rugby players, twice-weekly low-load knee extension with occlusion increased strength and fatigue resistance where the same load without occlusion did not, and knee extensor size rose in the occlusion group (size was not measured in the other groups). Staff could consider it as a supplement in supervised training, with occlusion pressure monitored as in this study.
paper.athleteDev: In elite rugby players, 8 weeks at about 50% 1RM with occlusion increased isokinetic strength and fatigue resistance more than the same load without occlusion, and knee extensor CSA rose 12.3% in the occlusion group. Size was measured only in the occlusion group, the groups were small, and sport performance was not measured.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested healthy trained athletes, included no injured participants, and measured no tendon load tolerance or rehabilitation outcome.

records.sourceFile: Electromyographic Comparison of Flywheel Inertial Leg Curl and Nordic Hamstring Exercise Among Soccer Players.pdf

paper.citation: Pedersen H, Saeterbakken AH, Vagle M, Fimland MS, Andersen V. Electromyographic Comparison of Flywheel Inertial Leg Curl and Nordic Hamstring Exercise Among Soccer Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Fifteen male amateur soccer players performed five repetitions each of the Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) and the flywheel inertial leg curl (FLC) in a randomised, counterbalanced order. Surface EMG of the biceps femoris and semitendinosus was recorded at three sites and analysed by lower and upper movement phases.
paper.tldr: In amateur male soccer players, the flywheel inertial leg curl produced similar hamstring activation to the Nordic hamstring exercise in the lower eccentric phase and higher activation in the concentric phase. It may be a more individualised option for weaker players, but this is an activation study, not an injury study.
paper.methods: Within-subject crossover design. Each player completed five maximal repetitions of the NHE (bodyweight) and of the FLC (load producing maximal power output), in randomised order. EMG was normalised to maximal voluntary contraction and root mean square values were compared between exercises by phase using paired t tests.
paper.findings: In the lower eccentric phase there were no significant differences between exercises (P = .101 to .826), although activation was non-significantly higher in all sites for the NHE (ES 0.08 to 0.61). In the lower concentric phase the FLC produced higher activation in all sites of the biceps femoris (31% to 52%, P < .001) and the semitendinosus (20% to 35%, P = .001 to .023). The NHE showed higher proximal semitendinosus activation over the whole eccentric movement (23%, P = .016).
paper.limitations: Only male amateur players were studied, so results may not generalise to elite players. Surface EMG is an estimate affected by cross-talk, and the authors note that the lack of significant differences in the lower eccentric phase may reflect limited statistical power with 15 participants. All players used their arms to push off in the NHE concentric phase, the FLC was unilateral on the dominant leg, and injury outcomes were not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: If the goal is high hamstring activation in the concentric phase, the FLC produced clearly higher activation than the NHE. In the lower eccentric phase the two exercises were similar, so the FLC may suit weaker players as a more adjustable eccentric option. The study measured activation only, so it does not show that the FLC reduces hamstring injury.
paper.athleteDev: The FLC load can be individualised to each player's maximal power output, and the authors suggest it may suit weaker players before progression to the NHE. The data show muscle activation, not strength or performance gains.
paper.rtp: The study used healthy amateur players and did not include injured athletes, so it cannot guide return-to-sport loading. It does not show that either exercise reduces re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Enhancement of Mood but not Performance in Elite Athletes With Transcranial Direct-Current Stimulation.pdf

paper.citation: Valenzuela PL, Amo C, Sánchez-Martínez G, Torrontegi E, Vázquez-Carrión J, Montalvo Z, et al. Enhancement of Mood but not Performance in Elite Athletes With Transcranial Direct-Current Stimulation. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019.
paper.abstract: Eight male elite triathletes completed a crossover, counterbalanced, sham-controlled, double-blind test of 20 minutes of anodal tDCS over the motor cortex or sham before an 800-m freestyle swim. Vigor was higher with active tDCS after stimulation and after swimming, while swim time did not differ between conditions (596 s active vs 599 s sham).
paper.tldr: In 8 elite triathletes, one session of anodal tDCS raised self-rated vigor but did not improve 800-m swim time. Treat the mood result as a small-sample signal, not a performance aid.
paper.methods: Eight healthy male triathletes (age 20 years, VO2max 71 mL/kg/min) completed two sessions one week apart, receiving either 20 minutes of active anodal tDCS (2 mA, anode at C3, cathode at Fp2) or sham. An 800-m freestyle swim test followed each session. Brunel Mood Scale, RPE, blood lactate, heart-rate variability and a CNS readiness score were recorded.
paper.findings: Vigor (change from baseline) was higher with active tDCS than sham after stimulation (P = .018, g = 1.14) and after swimming (P = .022, g = 0.98); other mood domains showed no condition effect. Swim time was 596 s with active and 599 s with sham tDCS (P = .346), and peak lactate, RPE, pacing, heart-rate variability and CNS readiness did not differ significantly. Tingling was reported by all 8 athletes in both conditions, with no difference in adverse effects.
paper.limitations: Eight men were studied, which the authors justify by the difficulty of recruiting elite athletes. The study used one stimulation protocol and a cephalic montage, and it did not measure cortical excitability or brain activity. Swim time was compared with a paired t test (P = .346) and with magnitude-based inference ('likely trivial'), and the authors note an extracephalic montage may work differently.
paper.practicalImplications: In this study, one session of anodal tDCS raised self-rated vigor but did not improve 800-m swim time. Any use with athletes needs replication and should not be presented as an ergogenic aid.
paper.athleteDev: A single tDCS session did not improve 800-m swim time in elite male triathletes (596 vs 599 s, P = .346). Its only signal was higher self-rated vigor, so it should not be presented as a performance aid.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy athletes only and did not assess injury, pain, symptoms or recovery outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Enhancing athletic performance with complex contrast training - A Delphi study of elite strength and conditioning coaches.pdf

paper.citation: Luders J, Gleadhill S, Garrett J, Bennett H. Enhancing athletic performance with complex contrast training: A Delphi study of elite strength and conditioning coaches. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2024.
paper.abstract: Thirty-eight elite strength and conditioning coaches completed round one of a three-round Delphi survey on how they prescribe complex contrast training to team sport athletes. Of 139 statements, 31 reached 80% agreement, including use in the preparatory phase, in-season and in power blocks, four sets per pairing, 85-90% 1RM with two repetitions in reserve for the strength exercise, and bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise.
paper.tldr: Expert coaches agreed on a set of complex contrast training settings for team sport athletes, including four sets, 85-90% 1RM for the strength exercise, and bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise. These are coaching consensus points, not tested training benefits.
paper.methods: Three-round Delphi survey run in REDCap. Round one used 14 open-ended questions answered by 38 coaches with ASCA level 2 or equivalent accreditation and team sport experience, and the answers were analysed thematically into 139 statements. Rounds two (37 coaches) and three (34 coaches) rated agreement on a 9-point Likert scale, with consensus set at 80% agreement within one three-point band.
paper.findings: Consensus (80% or more) was reached for 31 of 139 statements. Agreed items included use in the late pre-season preparatory phase, in-season and in power blocks, one in-season session per week, four sets per pairing, three or four repetitions at 85-90% 1RM with two repetitions in reserve for the strength exercise, bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise, and 2-3 minutes of rest from the power exercise back to the strength exercise. Consensus was not reached for general pre-season use (73.5%), rest from strength to power, or sex-specific prescription, and time efficiency and practicality as reasons reached 79%, below the threshold.
paper.limitations: The results are coach opinion (38 at round one, 34 by round three), mostly from Australia and New Zealand, with a mixed sport background. Repetition results are internally inconsistent: Table 2 marks three and four repetitions as consensus for the strength exercise but neither for the power exercise (79.4% and 81.1% unmarked), whereas the Discussion says four power repetitions met consensus and the Conclusions reverse the two. The Discussion also says inter-set rest did not reach consensus while Table 2 marks 2-3 minutes as consensus, and the Abstract presents time efficiency as a reason although it reached only 79%.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches can use the consensus settings as a starting point: four sets, three or four repetitions at 85-90% 1RM with two repetitions in reserve for the strength exercise, bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise, and 2-3 minutes of rest back to the strength exercise, used in the preparatory phase, in-season or in power blocks. The study does not show these settings improve performance, so staff should track their own outcomes before relying on them.
paper.athleteDev: Expert coaches agreed on four sets of paired exercises, 85-90% 1RM with two repetitions in reserve for the strength exercise, bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise, and 2-3 minutes of rest back to the strength exercise, with one session per week in-season. The consensus covers coaching practice, not measured performance gains.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It surveyed coaches about training prescription and did not address injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Enhancing team sports performance - A case study of the optimal post-warm-up time window.pdf

paper.citation: Abade E, Rodrigues Costa A, Parraca JA, Tomas-Carus P, Clemente-Suarez VJ, Gonçalves B. Enhancing team sports performance: a case study of the optimal post-warm-up time window. Sport Sciences for Health. 2024.
paper.abstract: In 19 college athletes, a team-sport warm-up was followed by tests of jump, 20-m sprint and handgrip, plus saliva markers, at 5 and 10 minutes after the warm-up. Jump and sprint improved from pre-warm-up to both time points, while handgrip did not change significantly. Salivary flux fell and alpha-amylase and protein rose, which the authors interpret as sympathetic activation.
paper.tldr: In a single session of 19 college athletes, jump and sprint were better 5 and 10 minutes after a team-sport warm-up than before it. Mean sprint time was best at 5 minutes, but the 5 vs 10 minute difference was not significant and there was no control group.
paper.methods: Single-day repeated-measures design with no control group. Nineteen injury-free college athletes completed a standard team-sport warm-up, then were tested before the warm-up and at 5 and 10 minutes after it. Measures were countermovement jump, 20-m sprint, dominant-hand handgrip and unstimulated saliva flux, alpha-amylase and total protein. Effects were analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc tests and Cohen's d.
paper.findings: Countermovement jump rose from 0.35 m pre-warm-up to 0.38 m at 5 minutes and 0.37 m at 10 minutes (F = 8.2, P < .001; small effects), with a trivial 5 vs 10 minute difference. The 20-m sprint improved from 3.83 s to 3.60 s at 5 minutes (large effect) and 3.68 s at 10 minutes (moderate effect); the 0.07 s slowing from 5 to 10 minutes had a 95% CI crossing zero (-0.01 to 0.16) and was not a significant post hoc difference. Handgrip did not change significantly (F = 2.1, P = .14), and salivary flux fell while alpha-amylase and total protein per litre rose, with amylase per mg of protein unchanged.
paper.limitations: There was no control group, so the results cannot show that the warm-up caused the changes rather than time, test order, learning or measurement drift. The Abstract says all three performance measures changed significantly (P < .001), but Table 1 shows handgrip did not (P = .14), and the Results still describe a 'late small increase of ~2 kg'. The saliva markers are used as indicators of sympathetic activity, which the study did not measure directly, and the reported body mass of 6.787 ± 11.57 kg is implausible.
paper.practicalImplications: Jump and sprint were still better than pre-warm-up values 10 minutes after a team-sport warm-up in this group, so a 5 to 10 minute gap before play did not erase the warm-up effect. Because responses varied between athletes and there was no control, check individual timing before changing a routine. The paper's suggestion of a re-warm-up is speculative and was not tested.
paper.athleteDev: In this single-session study, sprint and jump performance were above pre-warm-up levels at both 5 and 10 minutes after a team-sport warm-up. The mean sprint time was slightly slower at 10 than at 5 minutes, but that difference was not significant, so it does not establish a decline.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested injury-free athletes only, and it did not assess injured athletes, pain or readiness criteria.

records.sourceFile: Evaluating a 14-week neck strengthening protocol for neuromuscular indicators associated with head and neck trauma.pdf

paper.citation: Schroeder LH, Tyndall MC, McDaniel AT, Wang Y, Kale JL. Evaluating a 14-week neck strengthening protocol for neuromuscular indicators associated with head and neck trauma. Sports Medicine and Health Science. 2024.
paper.abstract: This pilot study tested whether a 14-week neck-strengthening program using a helmet-mounted device increased isometric neck strength and rate of force development in young adults. The authors report increases in rate of force development in both rotation directions and in isometric strength in cervical extension and left lateral flexion. They suggest the protocol may help reduce traumatic brain injury, but the study did not measure injury outcomes.
paper.tldr: A 14-week helmet-mounted neck program was followed by higher rate of force development on the device in healthy young adults, with less consistent evidence for isometric strength. There was no control group and no concussion outcome, so it cannot show an injury benefit.
paper.methods: Twenty adults consented and 18 (aged 18 to 29 years) completed 14 weeks of staged training on the TopSpin360 device, which uses self-generated centripetal force, in sessions of about 10 to 15 minutes. Isometric neck strength was tested in four directions with a portable tool, and rate of force development and revolutions per minute were measured on the device. Linear models regressed post-program scores on pre-program scores, and mixed models tracked change across sessions.
paper.findings: Rate of force development rose across sessions by 0.132 (clockwise) and 0.137 (counterclockwise) per session (both P < 0.001), and every participant's post value in Tables 5 and 6 exceeded the pre value. The pre-post analyses tested the slope of post on pre: slopes were 2.649 clockwise (one-sided P = 0.010) and 1.913 counterclockwise (one-sided P = 0.034), and the abstract's 4.344 and 5.978 come from the same model with one outlier removed. For isometric strength, slopes were significant for cervical extension (P = 0.010) and left lateral flexion (P = 0.009) but not flexion (P = 0.065) or right lateral flexion (P = 0.702); no mean pre-post change in kilograms is reported.
paper.limitations: There was no control group, training was short, and the small sample was recruited during COVID-19 restrictions with a narrow age range. The analysis regresses post on pre scores, so its slopes and P values describe how pre predicts post rather than the magnitude of change, and the authors interpret slopes as 'times greater'; some P values are one-sided, the abstract values depend on removing one outlier, and residuals were non-normal for right lateral flexion. Participant counts conflict (20 consented and 18 completed in the results, 18 consented in the methods, 19 and 21 in the models), and reference 19 is a patent for the neck assessment tool held by two authors, which the conflict statement does not mention.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could treat the staged 14-week protocol as an option for building device-measured rate of force development in healthy adults and should test isometric strength before and after with their own data. The study does not show that the protocol reduces concussions or brain injury and should not be presented as injury prevention.
paper.athleteDev: Rate of force development on the device improved over 14 weeks in healthy young adults, while isometric strength evidence was mixed across directions. The study does not measure sport performance or responses to contact.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. Participants were healthy adults without neck or head injury, so the study cannot inform neck rehabilitation, concussion recovery or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Exercise with blood flow restriction - An updated evidence       based approach for enhanced muscular development.pdf

paper.citation: Scott BR, Loenneke JP, Slattery KM, Dascombe BJ. Exercise with Blood Flow Restriction: An Updated Evidence-Based Approach for Enhanced Muscular Development. Sports Med. 2014.
paper.abstract: Review of the evidence on blood flow restriction (BFR) combined with low-load resistance exercise, with low-workload aerobic exercise, and at rest. It gives practical guidance on cuff type and width, restrictive pressure, exercise type, load, volume, inter-set rest and training frequency for clinical, healthy and athletic populations.
paper.tldr: Adding BFR to low-load resistance training (about 20 to 40% 1RM) enhances muscle and strength responses, and BFR alone can limit disuse atrophy. The authors give guidance on cuff width, pressure, volume and rest, and note that the pressure guidance needs more study.
paper.methods: Narrative review with practical recommendations. No systematic search method is described. The authors summarize acute and adaptive studies of BFR, then present a summary table of recommendations and a flowchart for clinical, healthy and athletic populations.
paper.findings: BFR combined with low-load resistance exercise enhances hypertrophy and strength, and BFR alone during cast immobilization can attenuate disuse atrophy. Low-workload walking or cycling with BFR gives small but significant gains in muscle size and strength. The summary table recommends wide cuffs for the legs and narrow cuffs for the arms, 50% to 80% of arterial occlusion pressure at rest, 30 to 45 s rest between sets, 50 to 80 repetitions per exercise, and 2 to 4 athletic sessions per week in addition to high-load training.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe a search method, and much of the cited evidence comes from small samples, often of untrained or older participants. Some pressure guidance relies on unpublished laboratory data, the circumference-based pressures have not been tested for training adaptation, and the authors state that the mechanisms are not yet understood. Strength gains after BFR are not larger than muscle size gains, and the Conclusions give 30 to 60 s inter-set rest while Table 1 gives 30 to 45 s.
paper.practicalImplications: Match cuff width to the limb, with wider cuffs for the legs, and set pressure for each limb rather than using one fixed value. Pair low loads (about 20 to 40% 1RM) with short rest (30 to 45 s, cuff kept on) and high total repetitions (50 to 80 per exercise), reducing intensity or lengthening rest rather than cutting set volume when the planned repetitions cannot be completed. Screen for contraindications such as a history of deep-vein thrombosis, pregnancy or varicose veins, and avoid regular training to failure for people new to BFR.
paper.athleteDev: Gives athletes a low-load, lower-mechanical-stress option that the authors suggest should be added to high-load training, not used as the only method. The review notes that strength gains after BFR are closer to hypertrophy than to neural adaptation, so it may not replace heavy strength work for athletic development.
paper.rtp: Relevant to rehabilitation, where the review suggests BFR at rest or with walking or cycling can limit disuse atrophy when high loads are not tolerated, following the four-phase progressive model of Loenneke et al. The review gives no return-to-sport criteria or outcome data showing when an injured athlete is ready to resume high-load training.
